prompt: What one question are indicators of compromise good at answering?

choices.text: Is the rule well tuned?
choices.why: Tuning is lesson 6's question.

choices.text: Who is behind the attack and what else will they do next week?
choices.why: An atomic value says nothing about intent or identity.

choices.text: How did they get in?
choices.why: That takes an investigation.

choices.text: Have we seen this here?
choices.why: Right. Fast, and nothing more.

prompt: Two files differ only in one character. What does the lesson's capture show about their SHA-256 hashes?

choices.text: The second one is longer
choices.why: Every SHA-256 is 64 hex characters.

choices.text: They differ only in their last character, matching the change in the file
choices.why: Hashes do not change locally; the whole value changes.

choices.text: They share nothing recognisable
choices.why: Right. One byte changes the whole fingerprint, which is why hashes are trivial to evade.

choices.text: They are identical, because the files are nearly identical
choices.why: Nearly identical files have unrelated hashes.

prompt: Match each indicator to its grade.

pairs.left: a pattern derived from a sample file
many accounts from one source, then success

prompt: Order these from cheapest to most expensive for an adversary to change, after the pyramid of pain.
Why does the lesson say to invest in detection at the top of the pyramid?
hint: What does the adversary have to do to evade it?

choices.text: They are cheaper to write
choices.why: They are more expensive to write.

choices.text: A detection there survives the adversary's next address
choices.why: Right. Changing a technique means learning a new way to work.

choices.text: Sharing groups only accept TTPs
choices.why: Groups share all kinds.

choices.text: Detections of TTPs never produce false positives in any environment, unlike lists of addresses
choices.why: They produce more, as the lesson says, which is the price of lasting.

prompt: What are the bottom layers of the pyramid still good for?

choices.text: Confirming quickly that a known thing is here
choices.why: Right. Fast and certain, for a short time.

choices.text: Nothing; they should be deleted
choices.why: The lesson keeps them for confirmation.

choices.text: Replacing behavioural rules
choices.why: They complement them.

choices.text: Predicting the adversary's next campaign from the addresses it used before
choices.why: Values say nothing about the future.

prompt: How many of 203.0.113.66's failures were for accounts that do not exist on gw?
Why is bruno's single publickey login an indicator of attack, when ana and diego log in by key every day?

choices.text: It is that account's first key login
choices.why: Right. The behaviour is new for that account, which means a key was added.

choices.text: The key was shared in lesson 8's report
choices.why: The report carried addresses only.

choices.text: It happened on a weekend
choices.why: It was a Thursday.

choices.text: Key logins are suspicious in themselves
choices.why: Two colleagues use nothing else.

prompt: Every nightly backup is bigger than the 612 MB transfer. What makes the transfer stand out?

choices.text: It used port 443, which the company's firewall normally keeps closed
choices.why: So does the backup.

choices.text: It came from files
choices.why: So does the backup.

choices.text: It happened at night, when nothing else runs on the network of the company
choices.why: The backup runs at night too.

choices.text: Its destination had never received anything before
choices.why: Right. The novelty is the signal, not the amount.

prompt: What is the price of behavioural indicators, according to the lesson?

choices.text: They expire within days, like the addresses they replace
choices.why: Behaviour lasts; values expire.

choices.text: They need a commercial feed
choices.why: They need a baseline of your own.

choices.text: They cannot be written in Sigma
choices.why: Lesson 4 wrote one.

choices.text: More false positives
choices.why: Right. A legitimate first-seen destination looks the same.

prompt: Match each of Thursday's steps to its ATT&CK technique.
hint: T1110 is credentials; T1021 is remote services.

pairs.left: many accounts, a few tries each
a large upload over HTTPS to a new address
a key the account never had

prompt: In ATT&CK, what is the difference between a tactic and a technique?

choices.text: There is none
choices.why: They are two levels of the catalogue.

choices.text: Techniques are older versions of tactics
choices.why: They are different levels, not versions.

choices.text: Goal against a way of reaching it
choices.why: Right. Lateral Movement is a tactic; SSH is one technique for it.

choices.text: A tactic is for Windows and a technique is the same idea written for Linux systems
choices.why: Both cover every platform.

prompt: Why does the lesson label T1098.004 with care?
hint: What do the logs actually show?

choices.text: It is a technique for Windows only
choices.why: SSH authorized keys are a Unix mechanism.

choices.text: The logs show a key login, not a key being added
choices.why: Right. It is the best explanation of the evidence, confirmed only on disk in lesson 17.

choices.text: ATT&CK withdrew it
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: It happened before the password login
choices.why: It came after, at 03:05.

prompt: Of the five steps mapped, how many did lesson 4's rules detect, and what does the mapping suggest writing next?

choices.text: One; a rule for the transfer
choices.why: Right. That was the step the investigation turned on.

choices.text: None; start again from scratch
choices.why: v2 caught the guessing and the login.

choices.text: All five; nothing more is needed
choices.why: Only the guessing-then-login had a rule.

choices.text: Three; a rule for weekend logins
choices.why: Thursday is not a weekend.

prompt: Written in a chat so nobody clicks it by accident, the address 203.0.113.66 is defanged as 203.0.113___66.
Why should a shared address carry a valid_until?

choices.text: So the SIEM can defang it
choices.why: Defanging is for human readers.

choices.text: To raise its confidence
choices.why: Validity and confidence are separate.

choices.text: STIX refuses to load any indicator that was shared without one
choices.why: The field is optional in STIX.

choices.text: It is reassigned to somebody innocent later
choices.why: Right. Old indicators block strangers.

prompt: A report lists an address belonging to a large cloud provider's shared front end. What does the lesson advise?

choices.text: Ask the provider for the attacker's identity
choices.why: That is not how sharing works, and they would not answer.

choices.text: Raise its confidence to 100
choices.why: Confidence does not fix collateral damage.

choices.text: Block it at once: cloud addresses are always malicious
choices.why: Thousands of legitimate customers share it.

choices.text: Prefer a domain or behaviour, since blocking it hits the innocent too
choices.why: Right. Shared infrastructure turns an address into a blunt instrument.

prompt: Next month, a different address tries 25 accounts on gw and one login works. Which of this lesson's detections still fires?

choices.text: The hash of Thursday's file
choices.why: No file was hashed, and a hash would change anyway.

choices.text: The behavioural ones: many accounts then success, and a first key login if one follows
choices.why: Right. They do not depend on the address.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: The behaviour is the same.

choices.text: The match against lesson 8's indicator for 203.0.113.66
choices.why: The address is different.
